lines.speaker: Πλούτων
lines.text: You know that old man—the really old one, Eucrates? The billionaire with no children and about fifty thousand people hovering around waiting for his inheritance?

lines.speaker: Ἑρμῆς
lines.text: Yes, the guy in Sicyon. What about him?

lines.speaker: Πλούτων
lines.text: Let him live, Hermes. Give him another ninety years on top of the ninety he's already had—more, if you can manage it. But those sycophants of his—young Charinus, Damon, the whole pack of them—drag them all down here immediately.

lines.speaker: Πλούτων
lines.text: Not at all, it’s completely fair. On what grounds exactly are they praying for his death and circling his money? They aren't even related to him. And the hypocrisy is sickening. They secretly wish him dead, but to his face they're falling over themselves to flatter him. He gets sick, everyone knows perfectly well what they’re hoping for, but they're out there loudly promising sacrifices to the gods if he recovers. It's a masterclass in sycophancy. So: make him immortal, and let them drop dead instead, with their mouths still watering.

lines.speaker: Ἑρμῆς
lines.text: [laughs] It’s going to be hilarious. They’re such hustlers. Eucrates plays them beautifully, you know—he strings them along, feeds their hopes... he always looks like he's on his deathbed, but he's actually healthier than the young guys. Meanwhile, they’ve already mentally divided up the estate and are living the high life on credit.

lines.speaker: Πλούτων
lines.text: Perfect. So let him shed his old age and grow young again like Iolaus. And let them be yanked right out of their daydreams, leave their phantom wealth behind, and come down here to die as wretchedly as they deserve.

lines.speaker: Ἑρμῆς
lines.text: Consider it done, Pluto. I'll go bag them for you right now, one by one. There are seven of them, I think.

lines.speaker: Πλούτων
lines.text: Haul them in. And let Eucrates attend all their funerals—looking like a twenty-year-old.
